questions.prompt: Write the single-ended CMRR of a symmetric resistor-loaded pair, the ratio of the one-output differential gain to the magnitude of the common-mode gain. \(R_D\) cancels. Use gm and RSS.
questions.explanation: The one-output differential gain has magnitude \(g_m R_D/2\), and the common-mode gain has magnitude \(g_m R_D/(1+2g_m R_{SS})\). Dividing them leaves \((1+2g_m R_{SS})/2\). Inverting the ratio gives \(|A_{CM}/A_{DM}|\). Using the drain-to-drain gain \(g_m R_D\) in the numerator, without the extra factor of 2, doubles this result. The estimate \(g_m R_{SS}\) drops both the \(1/2\) and the 1 inside the exact ratio. A differential output on a matched pair is a different case: that common-mode piece cancels, and mismatch sets the ratio.

questions.prompt: A pair has \(g_m = 1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_D = 20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) per side and \(R_{SS} = 200\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Taking one output, find the CMRR as a plain ratio.
questions.explanation: \(A_{DM} = g_mR_D/2 = 10\) single-ended and \(A_{CM} = -g_mR_D/(1 + 2g_mR_{SS}) = -20/401\). The ratio is \((1 + 2g_mR_{SS})/2 = 200.5\), about 46 dB. (The half-circuit gains are labelled prerequisites.)

questions.prompt: Order why a stiffer tail raises the single-ended CMRR. Each step after the first uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: CMRR is \(|A_{DM}/A_{CM}|\). Lowering \(R_D\) cuts both gains, and the single-ended ratio \((1+2g_m R_{SS})/2\) has no \(R_D\) in it. Setting the tail current to zero removes the bias rather than raising the ratio. Driving only one input does not change \(R_{SS}\). Capacitance across the tail does the opposite at high frequency: it lowers the impedance the common-mode half sees.
steps: In the common-mode half circuit each device is degenerated by \(2R_{SS}\).
Raising \(R_{SS}\) therefore lowers the common-mode gain, whose magnitude is about \(R_D/(2R_{SS})\).
The differential half circuit still has an AC ground at the source, so its one-output gain \(g_m R_D/2\) does not contain the common-mode gain just reduced and does not depend on \(R_{SS}\).
The ratio of that differential gain to the reduced common-mode gain rises with \(R_{SS}\). A cascode current source is one way to make that resistance large.

questions.prompt: A worked solution gives the CMRR of a perfectly matched pair whose output is taken differentially. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: Perfect matching makes the two common-mode outputs identical, so their difference is zero whatever \(R_{SS}\) is. A finite tail limits the single-ended common-mode gain, not this differential residue. Mismatch of the loads or of the two transconductances is what converts the common-mode current into a differential output. The supply voltage does not appear in that cancellation.
steps: A common-mode input pushes the same signal current through both matched halves.
The two drain voltages therefore move by the same amount.
A finite tail resistance still leaves a differential residue, so \(R_{SS}\) alone sets a finite differential CMRR.
Subtracting the two drains cancels that shared move, and any real differential residue comes from mismatch.
reasons: With perfect matching the differential common-mode gain is zero. A finite tail limits only the single-ended common-mode gain.
Matching does not matter. The tail resistance is what remains in the differential output.

questions.prompt: The pair has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_{SS} = 100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), and loads of 10.1 kΩ and 9.9 kΩ. A 1 V common-mode step is applied. Find the differential output \(v_{o2} - v_{o1}\) in mV.
questions.explanation: Each side's CM current is \(g_m/(1 + 2g_mR_{SS}) = 4.99\ \mu\mathrm{A/V}\). The 200 Ω load mismatch turns it into a differential output of \(4.99\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times200\ \Omega \approx 1.0\ \mathrm{mV}\).

retired_questions.prompt: A perfectly matched pair is read differentially. What limits its CMRR?
options: Nothing in principle: the common-mode output is identical on both sides and cancels; mismatch sets the real limit
retired_questions.explanation: With perfect symmetry \(A_{CM\to DM} = 0\); real CMRR comes from mismatch.
